explanation: SET NOCOUNT OFF leaves DONE_IN_PROC row-count messages enabled, increasing network traffic and client overhead.
SET XACT_ABORT OFF allows runtime errors inside transactions to leave transactions open or partially applied.
SELECT * on Sales.Orders retrieves all columns, increasing I/O and coupling callers to schema changes.
SELECT TOP (10) on Sales.Orders without an ORDER BY clause returns an arbitrary, nondeterministic set of rows.
DISTINCT is unnecessary on Sales.Orders.OrderID because OrderID is already guaranteed unique by its primary key.
WITH (NOLOCK) on Sales.Orders allows dirty reads, phantom rows, and missing or duplicated rows.
Applying YEAR() to o.OrderDate makes the predicate non-sargable and prevents an index range seek.
Comparing int column o.CustomerID to nvarchar variable @CustomerIdText forces an implicit type conversion.
The OR predicate (@CustomerID IS NULL OR o.CustomerID = @CustomerID) impedes index seeking and accurate cardinality estimation.
The leading wildcard pattern N'%urgent%' on o.Comments prevents an index seek and forces a scan.
NOT IN against a subquery on Sales.Invoices.CustomerID can return an empty result set if any NULL values are produced.
Wrapping o.CustomerID in ISNULL(o.CustomerID, 0) prevents direct index seeks on FK_Sales_Orders_CustomerID.
Performing arithmetic (o.OrderID + 0) on the primary key column prevents an index seek.
Inequality predicate o.CustomerID <> 1 is unselective and typically causes a broad index or table scan.
CROSS JOIN between Sales.Orders and Sales.Customers omits a join predicate and produces a Cartesian product.
Comma-separated tables Sales.Orders and Sales.OrderLines use legacy join syntax instead of explicit ANSI JOIN.
The correlated scalar subquery counting Sales.OrderLines executes per outer Sales.Orders row instead of using a grouped join.
The correlated EXISTS subquery on Sales.OrderLines can be expressed more clearly as a set-based join.
The CASE WHEN o.Comments IS NULL THEN 0 ELSE 1 END expression is duplicated in both the SELECT list and ORDER BY clause.
ORDER BY 2 relies on select-list column position, which is fragile if columns are reordered or added.
OFFSET/FETCH pagination orders only by non-unique o.OrderDate without a unique tie-breaker column such as o.OrderID.
UNION performs unnecessary duplicate elimination between mutually exclusive branches (OrderID = 1 and OrderID = 2).
Using (SELECT COUNT(*) ...) > 0 counts all matching Sales.OrderLines rows when EXISTS would stop at the first match.
SELECT @OrderID = o.OrderID from Sales.Orders silently assigns an arbitrary row when multiple rows match.
Table variable @OrderIds lacks column statistics and can lead to poor cardinality estimates.
SELECT ... INTO #ImplicitOrders creates a temporary table implicitly without an explicit schema definition.
Declaring and iterating order_cursor processes Sales.Orders row by row instead of using a set-based operation.
WHILE loop performs iterative row-by-row processing instead of a set-based query.
Concatenating @CustomerID into @Sql builds dynamic SQL via string concatenation instead of parameterization.
sys.sp_executesql executes @Sql without parameterized inputs, preventing plan reuse and safe value binding.
Temporary table #Scratch is explicitly created but never dropped before the procedure ends.
The CATCH block selects ERROR_MESSAGE() without rethrowing via THROW or returning an error status.
RAISERROR is used instead of THROW for raising an error on negative @OrderID.
PRINT is buffered and unsuitable for structured production diagnostics.
Hard-coded business identifier o.CustomerID = 1 is embedded directly in the query.
Unlabelled date literal '20160101' is embedded directly in the WHERE clause on o.OrderDate.
CONVERT(date, '01/02/2016') omits an explicit style code and depends on session DATEFORMAT settings.
Using COALESCE on o.CustomerID and i.CustomerID in the JOIN predicate inhibits index usage and join optimization.
Sales.Orders is self-joined on its primary key OrderID solely to retrieve the same OrderID already available in the outer table.
ORDER BY o.Comments sorts by an nvarchar(MAX) LOB column, causing expensive memory grants and tempdb spills.
SUM(ol.Quantity) aggregates the entire Sales.OrderLines table without any WHERE filter.
HAVING ol.OrderID > 0 filters rows after grouping rather than filtering before aggregation in a WHERE clause.
ORDER BY OrderCount is redundant because COUNT(*) without GROUP BY always returns a single row.
MERGE on Sales.Orders has known concurrency and edge-case bugs in SQL Server.
UPDATE Sales.Orders SET Comments = Comments writes the same value back, generating unnecessary locking and transaction log overhead.
DELETE FROM Sales.OrderLines filters by non-key column Quantity = -1 instead of a primary key.
WAITFOR DELAY '00:00:01' blocks a SQL Server worker thread synchronously.
BEGIN TRANSACTION is not enclosed in a TRY...CATCH block to ensure proper error handling and rollback.
SET IDENTITY_INSERT Sales.Orders ON alters session state and couples the procedure to manual identity management.
sp_who is invoked without an explicit schema qualifier.
SET ROWCOUNT 1 alters the session row-count limit without resetting it to 0 afterward.
INSERT INTO #DemoCategories omits an explicit column list, making the statement fragile to schema changes.
INSERT INTO #DemoCustomers omits an explicit column list, making the statement fragile to schema changes.
LIKE '%' + @CustomerName + '%' on CustomerName uses a leading wildcard, preventing an index seek on UQ_Sales_Customers_CustomerName.
User-supplied parameter @CustomerName is concatenated directly into dynamic SQL string @sql, creating a SQL injection vulnerability.
sp_executesql executes @sql without parameterized inputs.
sp_executesql is called without the sys schema qualifier.
UPDATE #DemoCustomers lacks a WHERE clause and modifies every row in the table.
Predicate o.OrderDate >= '2016-01-01' in the WHERE clause filters out NULL rows from LEFT JOIN Sales.Orders, turning it into an inner join.
Unlabelled date literal '2016-01-01' is embedded directly in the WHERE clause on o.OrderDate.
WHERE DeliveryMethodID = NULL always evaluates to UNKNOWN under ANSI_NULLS; use IS NULL instead.
Calling scalar UDF dbo.GetCustomerType(CustomerID) in the SELECT list forces row-by-row evaluation across Sales.Customers.
The CATCH block handles an error inside an explicit transaction without rolling back the active transaction.
The CATCH block selects ERROR_MESSAGE() without rethrowing via THROW or returning a failure status.
Hardcoded index hint WITH (INDEX = 1) on Sales.Customers overrides the optimizer and is fragile if index IDs change.
Query nests three levels of derived tables (t3, t2, t1) and should be simplified or refactored into a CTE.
WHERE CustomerName LIKE '%A%' uses a leading wildcard that prevents an index seek on Sales.Customers.CustomerName.
SELECT * from dbo.GetCustomerOrdersMulti couples the query to all columns returned by the function.
Calling multi-statement TVF dbo.GetCustomerOrdersMulti prevents query inlining and often causes poor cardinality estimates.
